Additive, Near-Additive, and Multiplicative Approximations for APSP in Weighted Undirected Graphs: Trade-offs and Algorithms
Liam Roditty, Ariel Sapir

Abstract
We present a + 2 ∑ i = 1 k + 1 W i +2\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}{W_{i}} -APASP algorithm for dense weighted graphs with a runtime of OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 2 + 1 3 ​ k + 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right) , where W i W_{i} is the weight of an i th i^{\textnormal{th}} heaviest edge on a shortest path between two vertices. Dor, Halperin and Zwick [FOCS’96 and SICOMP’00] introduced two algorithms for the commensurate unweighted + 2 ⋅ ( k + 1 CLOSE ) +2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right) -APASP problem: one for sparse graphs with a runtime of OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 2 − 1 k + 2 ​ m 1 k + 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\frac{1}{k+2}}m^{\frac{1}{k+2}}}}\right) and one for dense graphs with a runtime of OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 2 + 1 3 ​ k + 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right) . Subsequently, Cohen and Zwick [SODA’97 and JALG’01] adapted the algorithm for sparse graphs to the weighted setting, namely a + 2 ∑ i = 1 k + 1 W i +2\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}{W_{i}} -APASP algorithm with the same OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 2 − 1 k + 2 ​ m 1 k + 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\frac{1}{k+2}}m^{\frac{1}{k+2}}}}\right) runtime. We fill the nearly three decades old gap by providing an algorithm for dense weighted graphs, matching the runtime for the unweighted setting. In addition, we explore nearly additive APASP, where the multiplicative stretch is 1 + ε 1+\varepsilon . We present a OPEN ( 1 + ε , min { 2 W 1 , 4 W 2 } ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon,\min{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{2W_{1},4W_{2}}}\right\}}}}\right) -APASP algorithm with a runtime of O ~ ( ( 1 ε CLOSE ) OPEN O ​ ( 1 CLOSE ) ⋅ n 2.15135313 ⋅ log ⁡ W ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{2.15135313}\cdot\log W}}\right) . This improves upon Saha and Ye [SODA’24], which had the same runtime, yet computed a OPEN ( 1 + ε , 2 ​ W 1 CLOSE ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon,2W_{1}}}\right) -APASP. For pure multiplicative APASP, we begin by presenting a OPEN ( 7 3 + ε CLOSE ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right) -APASP algorithm with a runtime of O ~ ( ( 1 ε CLOSE ) OPEN O ​ ( 1 CLOSE ) ⋅ n 2.15135313 ⋅ log ⁡ W ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{2.15135313}\cdot\log W}}\right) . This improves, for dense graphs, the OPEN O ~ ​ ( n ​ m 2 3 + n 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(nm^{\frac{2}{3}}+n^{2}}}\right) runtime of the 7 3 \frac{7}{3} -APASP algorithm by Baswana and Kavitha [FOCS’06 and SICOMP’10], while introducing an additional ε \varepsilon to the multiplicative stretch. We further view this result in a broader framework of OPEN ( 3 ​ ℓ + 4 ℓ + 2 + ε CLOSE ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{3\ell+4}{\ell+2}+\varepsilon}}\right) -APASP algorithms, similarly to the framework of 3 ​ ℓ + 4 ℓ + 2 \frac{3\ell+4}{\ell+2} -APASP algorithms by Akav and Roditty [ESA’21]. This also generalizes the OPEN ( 2 + ε CLOSE ) \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\varepsilon}}\right) -APASP algorithm by Dory, Forster, Kirkpatrick, Nazari, Vassilevska Williams, and de Vos [SODA’24]. Finally, we show that it is possible to “bypass” an OPEN Ω ~ ​ ( n ω CLOSE ) \tilde{\Omega}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\omega}}}\right) conditional lower bound by Dor, Halperin, and Zwick for α \alpha -APASP with α < 2 \alpha<2 , by allowing an additive component to the approximation (e.g. a OPEN ( 6 ​ k + 3 3 ​ k + 2 , ∑ i = 1 k + 1 ) ​ W i \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{6k+3}{3k+2},\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}}}\right){W_{i}} -APASP with OPEN O ~ ​ ( n 2 + 1 3 ​ k + 2 CLOSE ) \tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right) runtime.).



Contents

Introduction

We study the classic
A
ll-
P
airs
S
hortest
P
aths (
APSP
) problem in a weighted undirected graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
with non-negative weights
w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R^{+}}
. Floyd-Warshall’s algorithm
[
32
,
22
,
30
]
solves APSP in
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3}}}\right)
time. Johnson’s algorithm
[
17
]
improves it to
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2}\log n+nm}}\right)
, which is still
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3}}}\right)
for dense graphs. Despite advances (e.g.
[
20
,
26
,
31
]
), no truly sub-cubic APSP algorithm currently exists. The fastest known one runs in
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n^{3}}{2^{\sqrt{\Omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\log n}}\right)}}}}}\right)
time
[
31
]
.

Facing this, an immediate question arises:
Can we approximate APSP in less than
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3}}}\right)
time?
To explore this, we properly define the problem of
A
ll-
P
airs
A
pproximated
S
hortest
P
aths (
APASP
). For parameters
\alpha,\beta
, the goal of an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP is to compute, for all
u,v\in V
, an approximate distance
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
s.t.
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\alpha\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)+\beta
. If
\beta=0
, the approximation is purely multiplicative, referred to as an
\alpha
-APASP, where
\alpha
is the
multiplicative stretch
; if
\alpha=1
, the approximation is purely additive, known as
+\beta
-APASP, where
\beta
is the
additive stretch
; otherwise, the approximation is “mixed”.

In weighted graphs, defining additive approximation in a meaningful way is a bit tricky. By scaling edge weights, we can show that any constant
+\beta
-APASP is equivalent to APSP. To overcome this, we explore additive stretches that depend on
w
. One approach is a
+\beta W
-APASP, where
W=\mmax{w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)}{e\in E}
. However, it might hold that most shortest paths use edges whose weight is much smaller than
W
, hence a
+\beta W
-APASP yields a very “weak” guarantee.

Cohen and Zwick
[
10
]
addressed this issue by defining
W_{i}=W_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

,

).

We consider the approach of Cohen and Zwick under a broader spectrum which generalizes the concept of equivalence between weighted and unweighted approximations. Consider an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP in an unweighted graph for arbitrary
\alpha,\beta
and let
f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)
be a function. The problem of an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)}}\right)
-APASP in weighted graphs is a
commensurate version
of the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP problem in unweighted graphs if, when the weight function
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)=1
for all
e\in E
, the additive stretch of the two problems is the same, that is,
f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)=\beta
.

Two algorithms
\mathscr{A}_{1}
and
\mathscr{A}_{2}
, with runtimes
T_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
and
T_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
, respectively, are
runtime equivalent
if
T_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)\in\tilde{\Theta}_{W}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(T_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)}}\right)
, where
\tilde{\Theta}_{W}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\cdot}}\right)
hides poly-logarithmic factors of
n
or
W
. An
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)}}\right)
-APASP algorithm
\mathscr{A}_{1}
for weighted graphs is a
strongly commensurate version
of an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP algorithm
\mathscr{A}_{2}
in unweighted graphs if
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)}}\right)
-APASP is a commensurate version of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP and
\mathscr{A}_{1}
and
\mathscr{A}_{2}
are runtime equivalent. Thus, as long as
\mathscr{A}_{2}
is not improved,
\mathscr{A}_{1}
is optimal. We consider the broad question:

Question 1
.

For an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP algorithm in unweighted graphs, what are its strongly commensurate versions
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta,w}}\right)}}\right)
-APASP algorithms in weighted graphs?

Partial answers are already known. Cohen and Zwick
[
10
]
had two
+2W_{1}
-APASP algorithm with runtimes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{3}{2}}m^{\frac{1}{2}}}}\right)
and
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
, matching the runtimes of the two
+2
-APASP algorithms in unweighted graphs by Dor, Halperin, and Zwick
[
12
]
. Since
+2W_{1}=+2
when
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)=1
for all
e\in E

Related Work

Cohen and Zwick
[
10
]
had a
2
-APASP algorithm with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{3}{2}}m^{\frac{1}{2}}+n^{2}}}\right)
runtime and a
\frac{7}{3}
-APASP in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
time. Both runtimes were improved by Baswana and Kavitha
[
6
]
to
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m\sqrt{n}+n^{2}}}\right)
and
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m^{\frac{2}{3}}n+n^{2}}}\right)
, respectively. Kavitha
[
18
]
showed a
\frac{5}{2}
-APASP algorithm with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{9}{4}}}}\right)
runtime, which was improved by Akav and Roditty
[
3
]
to
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{5}{4}}m^{\frac{1}{2}}+n^{2}}}\right)
time.

These multiplicative stretches were initially computed in an ad-hoc manner, each requiring its own tailored algorithm. The approaches for these APASP algorithms were developed without a unifying framework or a recognition of a broader underlying structure. Only later did Akav and Roditty
[
3
]
observe that these seemingly distinct stretches are, in fact, a part of a family of problems characterized by the form of
\frac{3\ell+4}{\ell+2}
-APASP that can be computed in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\frac{3}{\ell+2}}m^{\frac{2}{\ell+2}}+n^{2}}}\right)
time. For example,
\ell=0
indicates a
2
-APASP algorithm that runs in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{1}{2}}m+n^{2}}}\right)
and
\ell=3
indicates a
\frac{13}{5}
-APASP algorithm that runs in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{5}}m^{\frac{2}{5}}+n^{2}}}\right)
time.

A related problem is
M
ulti-
S
ource
S
hortest

P
aths (
MSSP
), where instead of computing all pairs of distances, we are given a set
S\subseteq V
of sources and we need to compute the distances from this set to any
v\in V
. We define an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-MSASP similarly to an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP. Let
\varepsilon>0
,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S}}\right|\in O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{r}}}\right)
and assume edge weights are from
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,1,\ldots,W}}\right\}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\infty}}\right\}
. Recently, Elkin and Neiman
[
16
]
a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP algorithm with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m^{1+o\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{\omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r}}\right)}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime.

Dory, Forster, Kirkpatrick, Nazari, Vassilevska Williams and de Vos
[
13
]
utilized the result of Elkin and Neiman
[
16
]
and the
2
-APASP of Baswana and Kavitha
[
6
]
. They achieved a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm with a
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{2.21235201}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime, which improves the runtime of the
2
-APASP of Baswana and Kavitha
[
6
]
for dense graphs. We generalize this
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm
[
13
]
and our own
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm, similarly to Akav and Roditty
[
3
]
, and present a unified framework of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{3\ell+4}{\ell+2}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithms.

An equivalent approach was taken by Saha and Ye
[
23
]
. They computed a
(1+\varepsilon,2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1})
-APASP. Their base case was
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon,2W_{1}}}\right)
-APASP with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\cdot n^{2.15135313}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime. We improve the base case and compute a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon,\mmin{2W_{1},4W_{2}}}}\right)
-APASP, in the same runtime.

Toolkit

Basic graph notions

Unless stated otherwise, we consider an undirected graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
with a non-negative weight function
w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
, where the weight of an edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\in E
is
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. Denote
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|V}}\right|=n
and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E}}\right|=m

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{1,2,\ldots,k}}\right\}

u\in V

and the set

of
k

from a vertex
u

u=y_{0},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{k},y_{k+1}=v
s.t. for any

:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y_{i-1},y_{i}}}\right)\in E
. The weight of a path is
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P}}\right)=\sum_{e\in P}{w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(e}}\right)}
. A path with the smallest weight is a
shortest path
and its weight is the
distance
, denoted by
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
. The distance between a vertex
u
to a set of vertices
S\subseteq V
is the distance from
u
to the nearest
s\in S
. That is,
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)=\mmin{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)}{s\in S}
. The
pivot
of

We denote by
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
the distance estimate computed by our algorithms. For an
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\alpha,\beta}}\right)
-APASP algorithm, we prove that
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\alpha\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\beta
. Since
G
is undirected, we assume that any update to
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
also updates
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v,u}}\right]
. This adds only
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)
per update and does not affect the overall runtime.

Nearest vertices and pivots

Figure 1:
The set
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,2}}\right)
, where
A=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}}\right\}
.

Given several sets
T_{1},T_{2},\ldots,T_{\ell}
of elements from a universe
U=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{n}}}\right\}
, a
hitting set
is a set
S\subseteq U
such that for any
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
:
S\cap T_{i}\neq\varnothing
. In our context,
U=V
and
T_{u}=\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,k}}\right)
for
u\in V
and some
k
that will be later specified. A hitting set, in this sense, is a set
S\subseteq V
of small size which contains at least one of the
k
-nearest vertices of
u
, for all
u\in V
. Hence its pivot
p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
is the nearest vertex between
u
and
S
. That is,
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,s}}\right)
for all
s\in S
.

Let
A\subseteq V
and
u\in V
. We can consider
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,k}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{a_{1,u},a_{2,u},\ldots,a_{k,u}}}\right\}
where
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,a_{i-1,u}}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(a_{i,u}}}\right)
for
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k}}\right]
, and for any
a\in A
:
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(a_{k,u}}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(a,u}}\right)
. That is, the nearest vertices from the set
A
(see
Figure 1
). These definitions are useful for APASP by distinguishing between pairs of vertices
u,v\in V
that are “far” from each other – and those that are “near” – that is, one lies within
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\cdot,k}}\right)
of the other. For near vertices, usually the exact distance is computed, by an algorithm
[
6
,
27
]
similar to Dijkstra, while for “far” vertices, we use an approximation on paths that pass through the pivots.

(

]
)
.

Let
r\in\mathbb{N}
such that
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|T_{i}}}\right|\geq r
for any
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\ell}}\right]
. A hitting set
S\subseteq U
of size
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{n}{r}}}\right)
can be deterministically computed in
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(nr}}\right)
time.

Observation 2.2
.

Let
k\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[n}}\right]
. The sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,k}}\right)
and the exact distances
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,x}}\right]=\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)
for any
x\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,k}}\right)
can be computed deterministically in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(kn}}\right)
time, for all
u\in V
.

The above can be extended for an
A\subseteq V
. By considering the
k^{\textnormal{th}}
nearest neighbour of
u
, we can iterate over members of
A\cap\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and select only those with a smaller distance to
u
.

Observation 2.3
.

Let
k\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[n}}\right]
and
A\subseteq V
. The sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,k}}\right)
and the exact distances
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,x}}\right]=\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)
for any
x\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,A,k}}\right)
can be computed deterministically in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|A}}\right|}}\right)
time, for all
u\in V
.

E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)}}\right\}
is the set of edges near
u
whose weight is smaller than
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S}}\right)
, and
E_{S}=\mcup{E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}{u\in V}
. We remark that if a vertex
u
has less than
k
neighbours, we include all its edges in
E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
.

Denote the edges
H_{S}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,u\in V}}\right\}
. If there are multiple hitting sets, we set
H=\mcup{H_{S}}{S}
as their union. When concerning a hierarchy of hitting-sets
S_{1}\supseteq S_{2}\supseteq\ldots
, we assume that
S_{i+1}\subseteq S_{i}
, and that each
S_{i}
has its set of edges
E_{S_{i}}
and pivots
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)\in S_{i}
for each
u\in V
.

Observation 2.5

(
[
27
]
)
.

Let

. Then:
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right|\leq k
. Additionally,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S}}}\right|\leq nk
.

We note that finding the pivots themselves and the exact distances from each vertex to its pivot, can be accomplished by a single SSSP invocation with an auxiliary vertex connected to
S
with edges of weight
0
.

Observation 2.6
.

Let

. The pivot

of each vertex

and the exact distance

can be computed in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
time.

Observation 2.7
.

The set
E_{S}
can be computed in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(nk}}\right)
time.

Observation 2.8
.

If
S_{2}\subseteq S_{1}
then
E_{S_{1}}\subseteq E_{S_{2}}
.

Min-plus matrix multiplication

M
in
P
lus
M
atrix
M
ultiplication
7
7

7

Also known as Distance Product (
DP
).
(
MPMM
) is a problem similar to
M
atrix
M
ultiplication (
MM
), yet uses a different multiplication operator: given two matrices
A
and
B
, their product
C=A\star B
, is defined to as:

C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i,j}}\right]=\min_{k=1}^{n}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{A\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i,k}}\right]+B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[k,j}}\right]}}\right\}

MPMM is runtime-equivalent to APSP
[
28
]
and is often used as a tool to reduce the runtime of shortest paths problems. However, MM and MPMM are not not known to be runtime-equivalent
8
8

8

If they would have been, as we already know
\omega<3
, we could refute the APSP conjecture.
. Nonetheless, faster MM algorithms can be utilized for MPMM by redefining the matrices (e.g.
[
24
,
33
,
9
]
). Since Strassen’s algorithm
[
25
]
, there was a series of works, many of whom in recent years (e.g.,
[
5
,
14
,
29
,
4
]
), which improved the runtime of fast MM. However, these algorithms “hide” large constants in their runtime.

Zwick
[
33
]
introduced
A
pproximated
M
in-
P
lus
M
atrix
M
ultiplication (
AMPMM
) in the same sense as APASP and presented a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-AMPMM algorithm with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\cdot n^{\omega}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime. That is, this algorithm computes a matrix
\tilde{C}
, where
C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i,j}}\right]\leq\tilde{C}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i,j}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[i,j}}\right]
. Bringmann, Künnemann and Wegrzycki
[
9
]
later utilized for a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\cdot n^{\omega}\cdot\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}}}\right)
time.

Overview

Common to all our algorithms is a hierarchy of hitting sets
V=S_{0}\supseteq S_{1}\supseteq\ldots\supseteq\varnothing
, where any
S_{i}\subseteq S_{i+1}
. Each level
S_{i}
has its own pivots
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for every
u\in V
and an associated edge set
E_{S_{i}}
(see:
Section
2.2
). The number and sizes of the hitting sets differs between the algorithms.

From the combinatorial perspective, our methods consist of selecting pivots through hitting sets and invoking multiple SSSP on graphs with sets of original and auxiliary sets of edges, tailored for the desired approximation. Some of our algorithms are order-sensitive considering the various SSSP invocations, as explicitly stated if so. We also consider distance updates through selected vertices, i.e. we have
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,x}}\right]
and
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[x,v}}\right]
and we update
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
.

Our main contribution in the combinatorial setting is our
+2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
-APASP algorithm for dense weighted graphs with a runtime of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right)
. Extending the
+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)
-APASP algorithm of Dor, Halperin, and Zwick
[
12
]
to the weighted setting gives rise to several challenges. First, we use
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,k}}\right)
instead of
N\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
. This change is required to ensure that if there exists an edge

. We emphasize that this issue    does not exist in the unweighted setting, where the upper-bound is simply
+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)
.

From the algebraic perspective, our methods consist of invoking
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP instead of several SSSP invocations, and
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-AMPMM for designated matrices. Note that rectangular MPMM can be used as a tool to replace distance updates through selected vertices.

Our main contribution in the algebraic setting is our unified framework of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{3\ell+4}{\ell+2}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithms with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(mn^{\beta}+n^{2+\gamma}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{\omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\beta-\ell\cdot\gamma}}\right)}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime. For dense graphs
m\in\Theta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2}}}\right)
, setting
\ell=0
results in the
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm of Dory, Forster, Kirkpatrick, Nazari, Vassilevska Williams and de Vos
[
13
]
, setting
\ell=1
results in our own
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm. For
\ell=2
we obtain a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{5}{2}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP algorithm with
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{2.1185119}\cdot\log W}}\right)
runtime. These results improve upon the framework of Akav and Roditty
[
3
]
for dense graphs, at the cost of an additional
\varepsilon
to the multiplicative stretch.

+2W_{1}
-APSP

An undirected non-negative weighted graph

.

A
+2W_{1}
-APASP.

as the edges’ weights and

(respectively,

) to be a hitting set to

Algorithm 1

+2W_{1}
-APASP
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)}}\right)

We begin by presenting
Algorithm
1
, which computes a
+2W_{1}
-APASP and has a runtime of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
.
Algorithm
1
can be seen as a a simplified version of a
\mmin{+2W_{1},+4W_{2}}
-APASP algorithm by Cohen and Zwick
[
10
]
, which had the same runtime. However, we omit the “
+4W_{2}
” part in-order to present a simplified case-analysis.
Algorithm
1
will later serve as a foundation for the generalized
2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
-APASP algorithm, namely
Algorithm
, that will be discussed in
Section
5
.

Algorithm
1
works as follows: we initialize a matrix
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
to be the weight of the edge for two vertices with an edge or
\infty
else-wise. We compute a hitting set
S_{1}
(resp.
S_{2}
) to the sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta}}}\right)
(resp.
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
) for all
u\in V
. For
S_{1}
(resp.
S_{2}
) we also compute its corresponding
E_{S_{1}}
(resp.
E_{S_{2}}
). We set
S_{0}=V
and
S_{3k+3}=\varnothing
, hence
E_{S_{0}}=\varnothing
and
E_{S_{3}}=E
. For each
u\in V
we find its pivot
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
(resp.
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
) and the distance
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]\leftarrow\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
(resp.
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]
) by a single SSSP invocation (See:
Observation
2.6
).

Let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left<2,1,0}}\right>
be an index
9
9

9

The order of
i\leftarrow 2,1,0
is of importance here, as will be argued further on.
.
Algorithm
1
invokes SSSP from all
s\in S_{i}
over the weighted graph
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E_{S_{i+1}}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V}}\right)\cup H\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(S_{2}\times S_{0}}}\right),d}}\right)
, where:

\blacklozenge

E_{S_{i+1}}
- The union, over
all

u\in V
, of edges
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
such that
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
,

\blacklozenge

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V
- Auxiliary edges from
s
to
V
, whose weight represents the distances that were computed in previous iterations,

\blacklozenge

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,u\in V}}\right\}
- Auxiliary edges from
any
vertex
u
to its pivots
p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{1,2}}\right\}
,

\blacklozenge

S_{2}\times S_{0}
- Auxiliary edges, , whose weight represents a distance that was previously computed, from
any
vertex
s_{2}\in S_{2}
to
any
vertex
u\in V=S_{0}
.

The weight of each such edge, whether auxiliary or original, is given by the matrix
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
. In other words, for any
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left<2,1,0}}\right>
and
s\in S_{i}
, the matrix
d
is a weight function over
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)
.

We emphasize that these SSSP invocations are performed in descending order from
i\leftarrow 2
to
0
, as auxiliary edges will have a weight given by
d
, which is a distance estimate computed in a previous iteration. To see that, recall that whenever
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right]
is assigned a smaller value than it previously held, the value
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]
is updated as well. Therefore, when an SSSP invocation from
v\in V=S_{0}
will occur, the auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
will be in use as well, and its weight is the previously computed value
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]
.

We now turn to prove the main theorem of this section:

Theorem 4.4
.

Algorithm
1
computes a
+2W_{1}
-APASP in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
time.

Proof.

The correctness follows by the case analysis and
Lemma
4.1
to
Lemma
4.3
. We consider the runtime. Initializing
d
takes
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2}}}\right)
time. Computing
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta}}}\right)
(respectively,
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
) for all vertices requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+2\beta}}}\right)
(respectively,
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+2\beta+2\gamma}}}\right)
) by
Observation
2.2
. Computing the hitting set
S_{1}
(respectively,
S_{2}
) can be done deterministically in
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta}}}\right)
(respectively,
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
) by
Observation
2.1
. Finding both pivots of each vertex and computing the distances to both pivots requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
by
Observation
2.6
. Finding the edge set
E_{S_{1}}
(respectively,
E_{S_{2}}
) requires
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta}}}\right)
(respectively,
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
) by
Observation
2.7
.

By
Observation
2.1
the size of
S_{1}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta}}}\right)
and the size of
S_{2}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)
. By
Observation
2.5
the size of
E_{S_{1}}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta}}}\right)
and the size of
E_{S_{2}}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
. As there are
n
vertices, the size of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V}}\right)\cup H
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n}}\right)
, which is smaller than any
E_{S_{i+1}}
. Additionally,
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{0}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)
. Implementing the SSSP invocation by Dijkstra, the runtime will therefore be:

\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{0}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S_{1}}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{0}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{1}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S_{2}}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{0}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{S_{3}}}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{0}}}\right|\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{2}}}\right|}}\right)}}\right)=\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\beta}+n^{2+\gamma}+n^{3-\beta-\gamma}}}\right)

By selecting
\beta=\gamma=\frac{1}{3}
, the runtime becomes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
.
∎

Additive
+2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
-APASP

In this section we introduce
Algorithm
, a generalization of
Algorithm
1
, which was presented in
Section
4
. Recall that
Algorithm
1
computed a
+2W_{1}
-APASP and had a runtime of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{\frac{7}{3}}}}\right)
.
Algorithm
extends this approach to compute a
+2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
-APASP, requiring
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right)
runtime
10
10

10

The case where
k=0
does not conform to the general runtime expression for
k>1
, analogous to the distinction observed between the
+2
-APASP and the
+2\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k+1}}\right)
-APASP algorithms of Dor, Halperin and Zwick
[
12
]
.
.

Algorithm
uses a parameter
k
that indicates a trade-off between the runtime and the approximation and parameters
\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{3k+2}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
, whose values will be determined as part of the runtime analysis. Our algorithm works as follows: for each
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
we set
\alpha_{i}=\msum{\beta_{j}}{j=1}{i}
and compute a hitting set
S_{i}
to the sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
, over all
u\in V
. For each
S_{i}
we also compute its corresponding
E_{S_{i}}
. We set
S_{0}=V
and
S_{3k+3}=\varnothing
, hence
E_{S_{3k+3}}=E
.

We initialize our distance approximation matrix
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
with edges’ weights or
\infty
otherwise. For
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
and
u\in V
we find the pivot
p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and set
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]\leftarrow\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
by a single SSSP invocation (See:
Observation
2.6
). We proceed with SSSP invocations from all
s\in S_{i}
over the weighted graph
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E_{S_{i+1}}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V}}\right)\cup H\cup F_{i},d}}\right)
, where:

\blacklozenge

E_{S_{i+1}}
- The union, over
all

u\in V
, of edges
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
such that
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
,

\blacklozenge

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V
- Auxiliary edges from
s
to
V
, representing distances previously computed,

\blacklozenge

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,u\in V}}\right\}
- Auxiliary edges from
any

u
to its pivots
p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
,

\blacklozenge

F_{i}
- Auxiliary edges from any
s_{j}\in S_{j}
to any
s_{\ell}\in S_{\ell}
, for indices
j,\ell
s.t.
i+j+\ell\geq 3k+1
.

The weights of these edges are given by
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
, which is a weight function over
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)
. These SSSP invocations are performed in descending order, from
i\leftarrow 3k+2
to
0
, since they rely on auxiliary edges whose weights were previously computed. To properly understand the reason behind this, consider a
u\in V
and let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
be the largest index such that
u\in S_{i}
. Whenever
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),u}}\right]
is updated, we also update
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right]
. Therefore, when
Algorithm
will invoke SSSP from
u\in S_{i}
, the auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)
will be considered as well, and its weight is the already computed value
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right]
.

whose weight is exactly

. Ergo, the recurrence in Condition (C) considers a different edge each time.

We now prove the second claim: for the number of recurrences of Condition (C). As we showed in each recurrence a different edge is considered, all that remains is to bound the number of edges, which is at most one more than the number of recurrences (if we halted due to Condition (B)). We consider two options:
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
and
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)>\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
. We begin with the first, and by the end briefly consider the second option. We provide two bounds, one when the relation halted due to Condition (B) and the other when it halted due to Condition (A).

and
\hat{\hat{v}}=\hat{u}
. Therefore,
\kappa(\hat{\hat{u}})\geq\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{u}}}\right)+1
and
\kappa(\hat{\hat{v}})=\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{u}}}\right)\geq\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)+1>\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)=\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{v}}}\right)
. In other words, in the first recurrence of Condition (C),
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{u}}}\right)
increased by at least
1
compared to
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
and
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{v}}}\right)
is equal to
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
. By the second invocation, both
\kappa(\hat{\hat{u}})
and
\kappa(\hat{\hat{v}})
increase by at least
1
compared to
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{u}}}\right)
and
\kappa\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\hat{v}}}\right)
, respectively. The value
\lambda\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

, as

from the first iteration rather than the second, which serves in our favor.
∎

We are now finally ready to state and prove the main theorem,
Theorem 5.3
, completing the correctness and runtime analysis of
Algorithm
.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}v}}\right)\leq 2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
. It follows that
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\msum{W_{i}}{i=1}{k+1}
. Observe that
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
always represents the weight of a path between
u
and
v
, hence
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)\leq d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
.

We now turn to consider the runtime. Initializing
d
takes
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2}}}\right)
time. Let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
. Computing, for all
u\in V
, the sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
requires
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
time by
Observation
2.2
. By definition:
\alpha_{i}<\alpha_{i+1}
. It follows that the total cost so far, for all
i
, is
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{3k+2}}}}\right)}}\right)
. Computing the hitting set
S_{i}
can be done deterministically in
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
time due to
Observation
2.1
, which means that the total cost remains
O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{3k+2}}}}\right)}}\right)
. Finding the
i^{\textnormal{th}}
pivot and computing its distance, for all vertices, can be done via a single Dijkstra invocation in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m}}\right)
time by
Observation
2.6
. This adds
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k\cdot m}}\right)
for all
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[3k+2}}\right]
. Computing the edge set
E_{S_{i}}
can be done in
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
time due to
Observation
2.7
, which means that the runtime remains
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{3k+2}}}}\right)}}\right)
. As
k
is constant, all the above remains within
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2}}}\right)
runtime.

By
Observation
2.1
the size of
S_{i}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1-\alpha_{i}}}}\right)
and by
Observation
2.5
the size of
E_{S_{i+1}}
is
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{1+\alpha_{i+1}}}}\right)
. Note that
\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}=\beta_{i+1}
. Hence, without taking into account the edges of
F_{i}
, all of the SSSP invocations from
S_{i}
require
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\beta_{i}}}}\right)
runtime.

We proceed to bound
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|F_{i}}}\right|
. Recall that
F_{i}
consists of
E_{S_{\ell}}\times E_{S_{j}}
for all indices
j,\ell
such that
j+\ell\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{3k+1-i,3k+2-i,\ldots,3k+2}}\right\}
. The corresponding cost of invoking Dijkstra from
S_{i}
over
F_{i}
is simply
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{i}\times S_{\ell}\times S_{j}}}\right|\in\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3-\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{\ell}}}}\right)
.

Fix
\beta_{i}=\beta\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
. Hence,
\alpha_{i}=i\cdot\beta
. Therefore, this runtime becomes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(i+j+\ell}}\right)\cdot\beta}}}\right)
. Since
j+\ell\geq 3k+1-i
, we have
i+j+\ell\geq 3k+1
, implying that this runtime bounded by
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{3-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3k+1}}\right)\cdot\beta}}}\right)
. We choose
\beta
such that:

2+\beta=3-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(3k+1}}\right)\cdot\beta

Which holds for
\beta=\frac{1}{3k+2}
. Therefore, the overall runtime of
Algorithm
becomes
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n^{2+\frac{1}{3k+2}}}}\right)
.
∎

Multiplicative
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP

Input:
An undirected non-negative weighted graph
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
and an
\varepsilon>0
.

Output:
A
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP.

Let
\beta,\gamma\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
to be fixed later

Initialize
d
as the edges’ weights and
\infty
otherwise

Compute
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,V,n^{\beta}}}\right)
(resp.
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,V,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
) for all
u\in V

Compute
S_{1}
(resp.
S_{2}
) as a hitting set to
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,V,n^{\beta}}}\right)\mid u\in V}}\right\}
(resp.
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,V,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
)

Compute the distances from any
u\in V
to its pivot
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
(resp.
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
)

Construct the set of edges
E_{S_{1}}
(resp.
E_{S_{2}}
)

for

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\in E

do

for

v\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,V,n^{\beta}}}\right)

do

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,1,2}}\right\}

do

d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),x}}\right]\leftarrow\mmin{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),v}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v,y}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[x,y}}\right],d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),x}}\right]}

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,1}}\right\}

do

for

s\in S_{i}

do

Invoke SSSP from
s
on
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E_{S_{i+1}}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V}}\right)\cup H,d}}\right)
and update
d
accordingly

Compute a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP from
S_{2}
on
G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)
and update
d
accordingly

for

u,v\in V

do

for

s\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{1},n^{\gamma}}}\right)

do

d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leftarrow\mmin{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,s}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[s,v}}\right],d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]}

for

u,v\in V

do

for

i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[1,2}}\right]

do

d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leftarrow\mmin{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right],d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]}

return

d

Algorithm 2

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E,w}}\right)}}\right)

In this section we present
Algorithm
2
that computes, for an arbitrary
\varepsilon>0
, a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
-APASP and has a runtime of
\tilde{O}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(mn^{\beta}+n^{2+\gamma}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{O\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1}}\right)}\cdot n^{\omega\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\beta-\gamma}}\right)}\cdot\log W}}\right)
, where
\beta,\gamma\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,1}}\right)
are parameters whose value will be determined when we will analyze the runtime.

Our algorithm works as follows: we compute the hitting set
S_{1}
(resp.
S_{2}
) for the sets
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta}}}\right)
(resp.
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)
), over all
u\in V
. We then compute the set
\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{1},n^{\gamma}}}\right)
(See:
Observation
2.3
). We compute
E_{S_{1}}
(resp.
E_{S_{2}}
). We also set
S_{0}=V
and
S_{3}=\varnothing
.

We initialize our distance approximation matrix
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
to hold either the weight of the edge or
\infty
. We find the pivots
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
(resp.
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
) for all
u\in V
and the exact distance
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]\leftarrow\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
(resp.
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]
) by a single SSSP invocation (See:
Observation
2.6
). We then update distances for
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)\in E
to the pivots
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
and
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
of all
v\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,n^{\beta}}}\right)
.

Let
i\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{0,1}}\right\}
. We begin with an SSSP invocation from all members
s\in S_{i}
over the weighted graph
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V,E_{S_{i+1}}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V}}\right)\cup H,d}}\right)
, where:

\blacklozenge

E_{S_{i+1}}
- The union, over
all

u\in V
, of edges
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
such that
w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)<\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{i+1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
,

\blacklozenge

\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{s}}\right\}\times V
- Auxiliary edges from
s
to
V
, representing distances previously computed,

\blacklozenge

H=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\,\middle|\,\,u\in V}}\right\}
- Auxiliary edges from
any

u
to its pivots
p_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
for
j\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{1,2}}\right\}
.

The weight of each such edge is given by
d:V\times V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}
, which is a weight function over
G_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(s}}\right)
. We then invoke a
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP from
S_{2}
. In contrast to
Algorithm
, the order between the invocations of SSSP and MSASP here holds no importance.

Finally, we perform two distance updates. The first is
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leftarrow\mmin{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,s}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[s,v}}\right],d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]}
for any vertex
s\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{1},n^{\gamma}}}\right)
; the second is by passing through any pivot of either
u
or
v
, that is:
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leftarrow\mmin{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right],d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]}
.

To prove a multiplicative stretch of
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)
, we follow the steps of the proof of the
\frac{7}{3}
-APASP algorithm of Baswana and Kavitha
[
6
]
. As we performed changes to their algorithm, we provide the reader with a full proof and a runtime analysis of
Algorithm
2
.

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our preceding discussion\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

Symmetrically,
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)
. Hence:
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)\leq 2\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Lemma 6.3
.

If
\case
a3 holds then
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Proof.

W.l.o.g.
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)
. Hence:
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)\leq\frac{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}{2}
. As we compute MSASP from
S_{2}
:
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)
and
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right]=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right)
. As we consider
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
as a pivot for
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]
:

\displaystyle d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right]}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Updating through the pivot of $u$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our preceding discussion\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}W.l.o.g. assumption\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(2+2\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing\end{tabular}}}}

By selecting
\varepsilon^{\prime}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
, we complete the proof.
∎

We can now delve within
\case
a2. Let us recall the vertices
x,y
from
Lemma
6.1
and the detailed case-tree previously presented.

We begin by addressing the “easier” sub-cases, namely
\notcase
b1 and
\notcase
b2, and then conclude
\notcase
b. This is done in
Claim
6.4
,
Claim
6.5
and
Claim
6.6
, respectively.

From there, we turn to
\case
b. Starting here, each time, we examine a certain condition. If it holds, we provide a brief proof. If it fails, we consider that sub-case and split it into additional sub-cases, repeating the approach, until we reach
\case
d and
\notcase
d.

We begin now by addressing
\notcase
b1. Throughout all the following claims, we assume, without loss of generality, that
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)
.

Claim 6.4
.

If
\notcase
b1 holds then
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq 2\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Proof.

Recall that after all the initializations, we update
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),y}}\right]\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
. Therefore, when we invoke SSSP from
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\in S_{1}
we will consider the auxiliary edge
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),y}}\right)
. The rest of the path
y\subseteq v\subseteq E_{S_{2}}
. Hence, we would reach from
p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)
to both
u
and
v
.

\displaystyle d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),v}}\right]}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Updating by $p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)\in\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,S_{1},n^{\gamma}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our preceding discussion\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$u\hbox to10.36pt{\vbox to4.99pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.56577pt\lower-0.7884pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}By our w.l.o.g. assumption\end{tabular}}}}

∎

Claim 6.5
.

If
\notcase
b2 holds then
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Proof.

Recall that we invoke
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP from
S_{2}
. In particular,
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right)
. We also update the distance through
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)
. Therefore:

\displaystyle d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right]}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Updating due to $p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right),v}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)$-MSASP from $S_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Due to \notcase{b}{2}\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

To finalize our analysis, we need to establish an upper-bound for
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)
. Let us recall what we know:

\blacklozenge

The set
S_{2}\subseteq S_{1}
and
y\notin\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S_{2}}}\right)
, hence:
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)
,

\blacklozenge

u\notin\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,S_{1}}}\right)
and therefore
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)
,

\blacklozenge

Due to our w.l.o.g. assumption:
\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)
.

Consider the path

Hence:

\displaystyle d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)\leq\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,x}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)+w\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,y}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}W.l.o.g. assumption and $y\notin\Gamma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,n^{\beta+\gamma}}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+\frac{\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}{3}}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Our preceding discussion\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\frac{7\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}{3}}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing\end{tabular}}}}\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\frac{7\varepsilon}{3}}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Simply summing\end{tabular}}}}

We conclude the proof by selecting
\varepsilon^{{}^{\prime}}=\frac{7}{3}\cdot\varepsilon
.
∎

Having proven both
\notcase
b1 and
\notcase
b2, we now know deduce
Claim
6.6
:

Claim 6.6
.

If
\notcase
b holds then
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Proof.

We have shown
Claim
6.4
and
Claim
6.5
. As either
\notcase
b1 or
\notcase
b2 hold, we conclude that
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.
∎

We now delve within
\case
b. We begin by proving
\notcase
c, in

6.7
:

∎

This leaves us with
\case
d from
Claim
6.9
:

Claim 6.9
.

If
\case
d holds then
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{7}{3}+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)
.

Proof.

Recall that we invoke
\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)
-MSASP from
S_{2}
. In particular,
d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),u}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),u}}\right)
. We also update the distance through
p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)
. Therefore:

\displaystyle d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,v}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right]+d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),v}}\right]}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Updating due to $p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)+\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right),v}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)$-MSASP from $S_{2}$\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle={\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Due to \case{d}\end{tabular}}}}

\displaystyle\leq{\underbrace{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\varepsilon}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(u,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,v}}\right)+2\delta\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y,p_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(v}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\begin{tabular}[]{@{}c@{}}Triangle inequality\end{tabular}}}}
